article.overview: A subsurface temperature sensor measures temperature at a known depth beneath the surface. The Moon's surface temperature swings by hundreds of kelvin between lunar day and night. Below a few tens of centimetres these swings are damped, and at depths of a few metres the seasonal signal is very small. A string of sensors at several depths therefore records how temperature changes with depth, which is the temperature gradient needed for heat-flow and thermal-model studies. Scope reading: this article covers the temperature-sensing element or string itself (thermocouples, platinum resistance thermometers (RTDs), thermistors and tether-mounted sensors that measure temperature in the ground). The heat-flow probe system is covered in payload 009 and the thermal conductivity instruments in payload 010; both are cross-referenced only where the sensing depends on them. The Apollo heat-flow probe temperature sensors are included as the catalogue entry suggests, but only the sensors are described, not the probe system. Five examples are covered, four of them flown: Apollo 15 heat-flow experiment temperature sensors (Moon, Apollo 15 site); Chang'e-4 in-situ temperature probes T1-T4 (Moon far side, 2019); InSight HP3 science tether with 14 PT100 sensors (Mars; the mole did not reach its planned depth); LISTER needle-sensor RTDs on Blue Ghost Mission 1 (Moon, 2025). The fifth, a Lunar Geophysical Network (LGN) RTD string on a pneumatically emplaced stem, is a proposal and has not flown.
article.description: A subsurface temperature sensor is a thermometer placed in the regolith, or in a probe pushed or drilled into it. Four design types appear in the sources. (1) Sensor strings on a probe or tether, in which several sensors are placed at fixed positions along a rigid cylinder or a flexible tether; Apollo, HP3 and the LGN concept use this approach. (2) Single or paired sensors on a penetrator or needle, in which a small number of sensors sit at the tip or along a needle inserted at successive depths, as in LISTER. (3) Surface-adjacent buried probes, thermistor probes within centimetres of the surface beneath a lander structure, as in Chang'e-4. (4) Thermal-element sensors, in which copper heater foils also act as resistance thermometers, as in HP3's TEM-A heaters. Platinum resistance thermometers (PT100 or similar) give a stable and well-characterised resistance-temperature relation. Thermocouples are robust and need no excitation current, but their accuracy is usually lower. Thermistors are sensitive over narrow ranges and need a calibration curve for each temperature band. The examples in this article use all three types.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose is to measure the temperature profile with depth. Combined with a thermal conductivity, the gradient gives the conductive heat flow from the interior. Where the depth is shallow, the same sensors record the daily and annual thermal waves, and the attenuation of the annual wave with depth gives the thermal diffusivity of the regolith (HP3 design basis). Sensors also support thermal models for landers and surface equipment: Chang'e-4 probes beneath the lander rails were used to examine how the regolith conducts heat near the surface. Sensors on a tether or string at several depths can separate short-period surface effects from deeper, long-period signals, which is a stated aim of the LGN concept.
article.operating_principle: A resistance thermometer uses the change of electrical resistance of a metal with temperature. For a platinum sensor of nominal 100 ohm at 273.15 K (PT100), resistance is measured with a known excitation current. In a four-wire (Kelvin) arrangement the lead resistance does not enter the reading. The HP3 tether uses this method, with a 100 ohm reference resistor measured in the same configuration. Apollo gradient sensors were arranged as resistance bridges: a pair of platinum elements in one arm gives a difference signal much more precise than the absolute temperature of either element. This is why the Apollo record reports a difference accuracy (0.001 K for high-sensitivity gradient differences) that is finer than its absolute accuracy (0.05 K over 190-270 K). Thermocouples produce a voltage from the junction of two different metals, read against a reference junction, usually in a temperature-controlled block. Thermistors show a large, non-linear change of resistance with temperature, so their readings are converted through a calibration curve. LISTER reads its needle-mounted platinum RTDs through a 24-bit analogue-to-digital converter over 100-400 K, which the instrument paper describes as giving resolution better than 0.001 K.
article.scientific_importance: A temperature gradient in the regolith is one of the two measurements needed for heat flow. It is also a direct record of how heat moves through the upper crust, which is linked to the Moon's thermal history. The Apollo heat-flow sensors produced an in-situ gradient record from the Moon, although the heat-flow results themselves belong to payload 009. The Chang'e-4 record shows the daily and seasonal temperature signal in the top few centimetres of far-side regolith. It tests thermal models of the regolith, but it does not describe the deeper gradient, because the probes were shallow. The HP3 tether was designed to measure a temperature profile to several metres on Mars, where the annual wave is small at depth. If its results are published in full, they would test the Martian thermal gradient at a depth that no lunar instrument in the sources read has reached.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power for a subsurface temperature sensor. The examples below use different sensor types, probe geometries and electronics. The data are not directly comparable, and values are given only for the named instrument and source. Where a value is not stated in the sources read, the article says so.

examples.name: Apollo 15 heat-flow experiment temperature sensors
examples.type: Historical lunar instrument (sensor set of the Apollo heat-flow experiment; system described in payload 009)
examples.status: Flown on the Moon at the Apollo 15 site. The Apollo 17 sensor layout was described in search results as a similar design, but its sensor counts and accuracies were not read and are not used here.
examples.probe_length_and_diameter: Each probe had two rigid cylinders of 50 cm each, joined by a flexible joint. Total probe length and probe diameter are not stated in the instrument description read. The 2.5 cm diameter in the record applies to the fibreglass borestem tubes, not to the probes.

platinum_bridge_sensors.cylinder_content: Each cylinder held four platinum elements forming two bridges: a gradient bridge (DTG) and a ring bridge (DTR).
platinum_bridge_sensors.absolute_accuracy_K: 0.05 K over 190-270 K (gradient and ring bridge sensors)

thermocouples.probe_thermocouple: One per probe, near the top of the upper cylinder, colocated with the top gradient sensor.
thermocouples.cable_thermocouples: Three per probe, at 65 cm, 115 cm and 165 cm from the probe thermocouple.
thermocouples.depths: not stated in the instrument description read

examples.reference_standards: Reference bridge in the electronics box: 0.01 K over 23-363 K. A reference thermocouple is in an isothermal block. No thermistors are mentioned in the description read.
examples.depths_as_emplaced: Probe 1: gradient and ring sensors between about 36 cm and 138 cm; borestem penetrated to 162 cm. Probe 2: sensors between about 3 cm and 96 cm, with one gradient sensor about 6 cm above the surface; borestem penetrated to 160 cm. An obstruction at about 1 m may have broken the borestem of probe 2, which would make the upper section and its readings unusable. All three cable thermocouples in each probe were above ground.
examples.sampling: A 7.25-minute measurement sequence in normal mode. In high-conductivity mode the ring-bridge sensors were read every 54 seconds.
examples.electronics: Electronics box nominally at 278-328 K; supplied with 29 V DC from the central station. Instrument mass not stated in the description read.
examples.heater_note: Heater settings (0.002 W and 0.5 W) belong to the heat-flow and conductivity work in payloads 009 and 010 and are not described here.
examples.notes: No direct image asset of the Apollo 15 temperature sensors or probe deployment was verified. A panoramic frame of the Station 8 ALSEP with the heat-flow experiment was identified in search results but not opened, so it is not used.

examples.name: Chang'e-4 in-situ regolith temperature probes T1-T4
examples.type: Flown lunar surface-adjacent temperature probes (far side)
examples.status: Flown on the lunar far side with the Chang'e-4 mission, 2019.
examples.mounting: Four probes (T1 to T4) held beneath the terminals of two metallic rails used to deploy the Yutu-2 rover, held by polyimide holders with a stated thermal resistance of about 5000 K/W.
examples.sensors: Each probe has two thermistors: a low-temperature type covering 77-223 K and a high-temperature type covering 223-523 K. Stated accuracy +/-0.3 K.
examples.burial_depth: No measured depth given. The authors infer from the timing of temperature rise after sunrise that all four probes are less than 1 cm deep.
examples.power: Solar panels by day and a radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG) by night, according to the paper's description. Probe power draw not stated.
examples.data_period: Data from roughly the second to the fourth month after landing; the 27 February to 28 March 2019 window is given as an example. Only probe T2, during the third lunar day, was used for the main analysis because the other nights gave discontinuous data.
examples.cross_reference: The paper also derives regolith density, particle size and conductivity from these readings. Those results belong to payload 010 and are not repeated here.
examples.notes: No direct image asset of the Chang'e-4 probes was verified. The image is left out rather than substituted.

examples.name: InSight HP3 science tether (TEM-P) temperature sensors
examples.type: Flown Martian tether temperature sensor array (HP3 instrument)
examples.status: Flown on Mars on the InSight lander. The mole attempted to burrow from 28 February 2019; the mission team ended its hammering efforts on 9 January 2021 without reaching the planned depth. Tether temperature-profile results are not described in the sources read (see data_quality_notes).
examples.sensor_type: Thin-film platinum resistance temperature sensors (PT100), nominal 100 ohm at 273.15 K, mounted on the science tether and connected in four-wire (Kelvin) configuration.

calibration_uncertainty_mK.status: Values differ between sources and are not reconciled.

examples.spacing_and_depth: Sensors are unequally spaced and denser towards the mole, to resolve the undisturbed gradient at depth. Sensors near the surface record the daily and annual thermal waves. The tether can reach a maximum depth of 5 m from its tip; the paper states that 3 m satisfies the mission science requirement. Individual sensor depths are shown in a figure and are not given numerically in the text read.
examples.readout: Two 24-bit analogue-to-digital converters with 8 differential channels each; seven channels per converter connected to PT100 sensors and one to a 100 ohm reference resistor. Sensors alternate between the two converters for redundancy.

mass_and_power.mass_note: Listed in Table 1 of the 2018 paper; the table is partly garbled in extracted PDF text and must be checked against the page image.

examples.mole_temperature_and_conductivity_sensin: Mole heater foils (TEM-A) are copper foils glued to the outer casing of the mole and protected by aluminium covers. Because copper resistance changes with temperature, the foils also act as temperature sensors. The NASA instrument page gives 12 TEM-A heating foils and a 1-sigma uncertainty of 30 mK. These belong mainly to the conductivity work in payload 010.

examples.name: LISTER needle-sensor RTDs (Blue Ghost Mission 1)
examples.type: Flown lunar subsurface thermal probe (needle sensor on a pneumatic excavation system)
examples.status: Flown on the Moon. Deployed in Mare Crisium on Blue Ghost Mission 1; landing 2 March 2025; LISTER operations from 4 March 2025.
examples.sensors: Two resistance temperature detectors (RTDs) in the needle sensor. RTD1 is a platinum RTD at the midpoint of the heater that spans the full needle length. RTD2 is described only as a spare RTD, and its material is not stated. RTD1 is calibrated for 0.01 K absolute accuracy.
examples.resolution: A 24-bit analogue-to-digital converter over 100-400 K, with resolution better than 0.001 K according to the paper.
examples.measurement_method: Measurements at eight depths. At each target depth, gas flow stops and the needle is used for thermal measurements before excavation resumes. Heater: Manganin resistance wire at 50 mW when active. Sequence: 1 h equilibration, 30 min heating, 30 min cooling (2 h total).
examples.depth_reached: The abstract and introduction state 1 m. Section 5 of the same paper states that LISTER reached 98 cm in its first three days and then met obstacles it could not overcome. Reported as 98 cm to about 1 m.
examples.mass: Total LISTER mass 12.9 kg including avionics (paper Section 3). Needle-sensor mass not stated.
examples.power: Total power not stated; the only stated power figure is the 50 mW needle heater.
examples.dimensions: Needle sensor 2.8 mm outside diameter with a 28 mm exposed length; stainless steel tube 6.4 mm in diameter; spacer-nozzle 10 cm long with 1 cm outside diameter. Overall mechanism and avionics dimensions not stated.
examples.heat_flow_result: Not reported in the primary paper, which states that the thermal data analysis is presented in another article. A news report of a conference talk says the heat flow at the site was comparable to Apollo 15 and 17 values; this is not used as a numerical value.
examples.notes: A flight-imagery frame credited to Firefly Aerospace and NASA Marshall was identified in search results but not opened, so it is not used. No direct, verified image of the flight needle sensor is included.

examples.name: Proposed Lunar Geophysical Network RTD string on a pneumatically emplaced stem
examples.type: Proposed concept (LGN heat-flow probe; not flown)
examples.status: Proposed concept. No flight unit described in the sources read.
examples.concept: A stem is extended from a pneumatic reel, and a conical tip is pushed into the soil while gas jets loosen the regolith. Thermal sensors are attached along the stem and at the tip. The conductivity sensor is a needle at the cone tip, described as 1 to 1.5 cm long, with an RTD and heater wire.
examples.sensor_spacing: The 2012 abstract proposes RTDs spaced about 30 cm apart along the stem to monitor long-term subsurface temperature, to separate diurnal, annual and precession-related thermal cycles from internal heat flow.
examples.accuracy: not publicly specified in the abstract
examples.mass_and_power: not publicly specified; the abstract says only that the system weighs about the same as a mole-based system.
examples.unverified_detail: A separate LGN requirements document, found in search results but not read, is reported to call for temperature measurements every 20 cm to a depth of at least 3 m (relative accuracy 0.01 K). This is not used as a verified value.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions differ strongly between examples. The Apollo probe was two 50 cm cylinders on a flexible joint with a 2.5 cm borestem; the HP3 science tether is a flexible sensor-bearing tether whose mass is discussed under mass_and_weight; LISTER's needle sensor is 2.8 mm in outside diameter and 28 mm exposed. Total probe lengths are not stated for Apollo or for LISTER, and the LGN stem is a concept. A new sensor string would need its dimensions set by its intended depth, sensor spacing and emplacement method.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: For the examples: Apollo 15 probe mass not publicly specified in the description read; HP3 science tether listed at 75 g in Table 1 of Spohn et al. (2018), subject to verification; LISTER total mass 12.9 kg including avionics (Nagihara et al. 2025); Chang'e-4 probe mass not stated; LGN concept mass not publicly specified. These values are not comparable because they describe different system boundaries.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Apollo 15: electronics supplied with 29 V DC from the central station; heater powers belong to payloads 009 and 010. Chang'e-4: solar panels by day and RTG by night, with no probe power figure stated. HP3: heater power is commandable between 0 and 1 W for the TEM-A foils; tether sensor power not stated. LISTER: only the 50 mW needle heater is stated; total power not given. LGN: not publicly specified.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Subsurface sensors operate in vacuum and in strong thermal gradients. The Apollo electronics box was held at a nominal 278-328 K. The Chang'e-4 probes were powered by solar panels by day and an RTG at night, and their polyimide holders had a stated thermal resistance of about 5000 K/W. Sensor accuracy depends on keeping reference junctions and bridges at known temperatures: the Apollo design used a reference bridge in the electronics box and an isothermal block for the reference thermocouple, and HP3 used four-wire readout to remove lead resistance. Thermal settling is needed before a gradient can be trusted; probes that are heated, or close to lander structures, record disturbed temperatures until they settle. Heater power must be low enough not to disturb the regolith being measured. Mechanical contact between the sensor and the ground matters: poor contact, or a string not seated against the wall of the hole, produces errors. The LGN concept proposes low-conductivity stem materials and close RTD-to-wall contact to limit conduction errors.
article.limitations: Sensor placement limits the measurement. Apollo's sensors were placed at fixed depths in holes drilled for the probes, and some were above the surface because of the emplacement. Chang'e-4's probes were shallower than 1 cm, so they cannot give a deep gradient. The depth of a sensor string is limited by the emplacement method: HP3's mole was designed to reach 3 to 5 m with a tether but did not reach the planned depth; LISTER reached about 1 m against a 3 m design goal. Calibration and reference uncertainties differ between instruments and sources: the HP3 tether uncertainty is 6.5 mK in the 2018 abstract and 12 mK on a NASA instrument page; the LISTER 0.01 K value is the paper's stated absolute accuracy at the sensor and does not include the uncertainties of the conductivity method. Sensors can be affected by the thermal behaviour of their support: the HP3 tether minimises copper cross-section to avoid heat shunting, and the Chang'e-4 holders have a stated thermal resistance; heat shunting along a tether or stem can bias a gradient.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A subsurface temperature sensor may be delivered to the Moon as part of a dedicated probe, a heat-flow package, or a lander payload. Transport and deployment requirements depend strongly on the design. Surface payload steps: integration into a lander, launch, lunar transfer, landing delivery, deployment into the regolith, and connection of power and data interfaces. The sensor string must be emplaced in a hole or driven into the regolith, and its depth must be known. Orbiter payload: not applicable, because subsurface temperature sensors are surface or near-surface instruments. Rover or mobile payload: no rover-mounted subsurface temperature sensor is covered in the sources read beyond the Chang'e-4 rover-deployment rails.
transportation_process: Integrate the sensor string or probe into a lander or a heat-flow package on Earth.
Launch and transfer to the Moon.
Deliver to the surface by a lander.
Emplace the sensor string in the regolith by the chosen method, such as drilled holes, hammering with a tether, or pneumatic excavation.
Set the power and data interfaces needed for the sensors and the heating or measurement sequence.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo 15: probes placed into holes drilled in the regolith, as described in search results on the Apollo 15 heat-flow experiment; sensor depths as emplaced are recorded in the instrument description. Chang'e-4: probes held beneath rails used for rover deployment and powered from the lander's solar and RTG supply; burial depth less than 1 cm (inferred). HP3: a self-hammering mole pulls a tether with fixed sensor positions behind it; a tether length monitor and static tiltmeter trace the path. LISTER: nitrogen gas jets loosen and eject regolith while the needle takes measurements at target depths. LGN concept: a pneumatic reel extends a stem with a conical tip while gas jets loosen the soil.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 15 heat-flow experiment (drilled holes, astronaut-placed probes); Chang'e-4 far-side probes beneath the rover-deployment rails; InSight HP3 hammering mole with a science tether (mole did not reach its planned depth); LISTER on Blue Ghost Mission 1 (pneumatic excavation to about 1 m).
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lunar lander, rover or spacecraft has been assessed here for compatibility with any of these sensors. Mass, dimensions, mounting, deployment loads, power and data interfaces would need to be compared with verified lander specifications before any assignment is made. Payload 011 does not assert compatibility with any named lander.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 15 and Apollo 17 heat-flow experiments produced in-situ records of temperature with depth in lunar regolith, using platinum bridges and thermocouples. The Chang'e-4 probes are a more recent example of in-situ regolith temperature measurement on the lunar far side, and their data cover the daily and seasonal near-surface signal. The HP3 tether was designed to measure a temperature profile to several metres on Mars. Its mole did not reach the planned depth, and its tether profile results are not described in the sources read. LISTER reached about 1 m with a needle-sensor temperature and conductivity measurement at eight depths. The paper describes it as the first robotically deployed subsurface thermal probe that excavates lunar regolith while measuring at several depths, and as exceeding the earlier robotic record of 8 cm.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Apollo 17 layout not read; the Apollo 15 sensor description is used as the Apollo example. Apollo 15 total probe length and diameter are not stated in the instrument description read; payload 009 records a conflict in Apollo probe length, which is not reconciled here. Chang'e-4 burial depth is inferred, not measured, and probe mass, dimensions and power draw are not stated. HP3 tether calibration uncertainty is 6.5 mK (2018 abstract) and 12 mK (NASA instrument page), and the difference is not resolved. HP3 tether profile data: a NASA instrument page states that after the mole failed to deploy, the radiometer became the only HP3 data in the archive; this is not reconciled with the 2021 HP3 conductivity result cited in payload 010, so the status of archived tether temperature data is unverified. The HP3 Table 1 mass of 75 g is taken from partly garbled extracted text. The 2021 and 2022 HP3 mole papers were not read in full. LISTER depth is given as both 1 m and 98 cm in the paper. The LISTER heat-flow value is a news report of a conference talk; the primary heat-flow paper was not read. LISTER total power is not stated. The LGN depth and spacing come from a 2012 abstract; the LGN requirements document was not read. No Chang'e-7 subsurface temperature sensor was found in search. Two verified images are used, both HP3 hardware rather than the sensors in place; no verified photograph of a lunar subsurface temperature sensor in place was found.

data_quality_notes: Scope reading: payload 011 is read as the subsurface temperature-sensing element or string (thermocouples, RTDs, thermistors and tether-mounted sensors). The heat-flow probe system (payload 009) and the thermal conductivity probe (payload 010) are excluded except as cross-references. The Apollo heat-flow probe temperature sensors are included as the catalogue entry suggests, described as sensors only.
Catalogue check: ID 11, name 'Subsurface temperature sensor' and category 1 'Geophysical and lunar interior instruments' match lunar_payloads_catalogue_320.md line 18 (entry 11).

Flight status: four examples flown (Apollo 15 sensor set, Chang'e-4 T1-T4, InSight HP3 science tether, LISTER on Blue Ghost Mission 1) and one proposed (LGN RTD string). Apollo 17 sensor layout not verified; the Apollo 17 instrument is not used as a numerical example.
HP3 tether calibration uncertainty conflict: 6.5 mK (1-sigma, Spohn et al. 2018 abstract) versus 12 mK (NASA instrument page). Both are reported; neither is resolved.

HP3 archive conflict: the NASA instrument page states that after mole failure the radiometer became the only HP3 data in the archive. This is not reconciled with the published 2021 HP3 conductivity result cited in payload 010, so the status of archived tether temperature-profile data is unverified. Tether profile results are not reported in the sources read.

HP3 Table 1 mass (science tether 75 g) is taken from partly garbled extracted PDF text and must be checked against the page image of Spohn et al. (2018) before reuse. Spacing and depth of individual tether sensors are shown only in a figure and are not stated numerically.
HP3 mole papers from 2021 (Grott et al.) and 2022 were not read in full. Mole temperature sensing is described only through the TEM-A heater foils.

Apollo 15 sensor values (accuracies, spacings, depths, sampling, electronics) come from a text-fetch summary of the PDS instrument description; the PDS text should be checked before reuse. Total probe length and diameter, and the instrument mass, are not stated in that description. Probe-length conflict recorded in payload 009 is not reconciled here.

Chang'e-4 probe depth (less than 1 cm) is an inference by the authors from the timing of temperature rise, not a measurement. Probe mass, dimensions and power draw are not stated in the paper as read. The paper's conductivity and density estimates belong to payload 010 and are not repeated.

LISTER depth conflict: the abstract and introduction state 1 m, while Section 5 states 98 cm in the first three days. Both are reported. The primary paper gives eight measurement depths and a total mass of 12.9 kg including avionics; LISTER total power and needle-sensor mass are not stated. The LISTER heat-flow value is from a news report of a conference talk and is not used; the primary heat-flow paper was not read. The second RTD's material is not stated.

LGN concept: the 3 m depth and 30 cm RTD spacing come from a 2012 NASA abstract. The LGN requirements document reported in search results (20 cm spacing, 0.01 K relative accuracy) was not read and is not used. Accuracy, mass and power are not publicly specified in the abstract.
Chang'e-7: a search found no source describing a Chang'e-7 subsurface temperature probe, planned or otherwise. No Chang'e-7 example is included.

Images: two direct images are verified (PIA24263 and PIA23272, NASA Photojournal, both HTTP 200 with image/jpeg). Both show HP3 hardware rather than sensors in place, and neither page establishes that the tether temperature sensors are visible.
